.Subject: A Personal Reflection on Playlist Visibility and Inclusion on Suno

Dear Suno Team,

First of all, I’d like to extend my appreciation. Suno stands out as the leading AI music platform, and I truly admire the innovation and creativity it enables.

I’m writing with a few thoughts, questions, and suggestions—mainly about how playlists are curated on the platform. I’ve noticed that the same users and songs appear frequently in featured playlists. This made me wonder: who is responsible for creating these playlists, and what criteria are used in selecting songs? With so many great creators on Suno, including many paying subscribers, it feels a bit discouraging to see such limited rotation.

At one point, I found myself trying to engage with playlist curators by liking and commenting on their songs, hoping to be noticed. But over time, that felt a bit unnatural. I don’t want my presence to rely on chasing attention—it would feel far more meaningful to be included through a more diverse and inclusive system. Even one feature can mean a lot.

For example, one of my songs was once featured in the “Best of Suno v4.5” playlist. I was truly honored and grateful. The impact was incredible: my followers doubled in just two days, and the song reached over twenty thousand plays. I also received messages from around the world. That single moment gave me an enormous confidence boost—not just as a user, but as an artist.

In fact, I’ve had two of my songs featured in the “Best of Suno v4.5” playlist—but only for a very limited time. The first was visible for just twenty-four hours before being removed, and shortly after, a second song of mine was added, also for twenty-four hours. In total, my songs were featured for just forty-eight hours combined. During that short window, the first song received over eighteen thousand plays, and the second reached over twelve thousand. Since then, the combined total has only grown by about one thousand plays in the week that followed. That kind of drop-off shows just how impactful a playlist feature is—and how fleeting that exposure can be if not given time to breathe.

After being featured, I started receiving messages from others asking for support—likes, comments, listens. I suddenly saw the system from another side. I can only imagine how overwhelming that must be for playlist curators and influencers on the platform. I really do understand and respect that. But it also left me unsure of how to be considered again, without having to push or perform for attention.

In the beginning, my engagement with other creators was entirely genuine. I was moved by the stories behind their songs. There’s something deeply human about what people share through their music on Suno—it’s often raw, emotional, and deeply personal. I even came across a creator who composed songs without hearing, using only the written lyrics and listener feedback. That touched me deeply. It reminded me this platform isn’t just about trends—it’s about expression and connection.

That’s why I care—not just about being featured again myself, but about seeing all kinds of unique, unheard voices lifted up. My own feature inspired me to create more, to buy extra credits, and to engage more meaningfully with the community. But over time, I noticed that my comments and interactions started to shift—I was no longer just connecting, I was trying to be seen again. And that made me pause.

One more thing I want to make really clear. Right now, after liking around 10 songs, I get a message saying, “You’ve reached your like limit”—and I have to pause. So I know the system already has the power and technology to control how we interact. But in my opinion, that limit should apply after each song, not after 10.

Instead of letting people rush through and like 10 tracks in a row, why not slow it down just a little? For example, after liking one song, there could be a short pause—maybe 30 seconds or 1 minute—before they can like another. That would encourage people to actually listen first, think about how the song made them feel, and then decide whether to like it or not. That’s what I try to do. But when people tap 5 or 10 likes in a few seconds, I know they didn’t listen—and it creates pressure to go return the gesture, even if it wasn’t real. I believe this kind of change would gently shift the entire culture of the platform toward more thoughtful, honest engagement. And it would make the algorithm smarter and more human at the same time.

There’s one more layer to this I want to express clearly: the like-for-like culture itself doesn’t really belong on a platform like Suno. That kind of system makes sense for platforms like Instagram, Facebook, or Twitter—where you can scroll through dozens of images or posts in a minute. You can quickly read a line, glance at a picture, and know whether you want to like it. The content is visual and instant. There’s light, there’s recognition, there’s a quick response.

But music isn’t like that. You can’t decide whether you like a song just by glancing at it. You have to actually listen, often for two or three minutes, to understand how it feels and whether it resonates with you. Songs ask for emotional presence. They carry stories. They take time.

That’s why the current system—where you can like 5 or 10 songs in quick succession and then wait 30 seconds before doing it again—just doesn’t work. It encourages people to skim, like, and move on, without engaging with the music itself. If I have two hours and I genuinely want to support a hundred artists, I still don’t know if that effort will reflect in the algorithm in a way that actually helps me too. I might boost others—and I want to—but I don’t know whether anything about my visibility improves through that.

We need an algorithm that’s fair—not just fast. One that understands music is not a scrollable feed. It’s a deeper experience.

I guess what I’m trying to say is: I just want to reach more people. I also have something to say. My music isn’t just for dancing or clubbing—though I respect those, too. It’s about emotion. It’s about being honest, helping someone feel stronger, less alone, more understood. I know my music will speak to people—if only they had a chance to hear it.

I hope this message is received in the spirit it’s meant: with gratitude, honesty, and belief in the Suno vision. I appreciate the opportunity to be part of this community, and I hope for a future where visibility and recognition are more widely shared among the diverse voices that make Suno so special.

Warm regards,
Mehmet Bagbozan

**Subject: A Personal Reflection on Playlist Visibility and Inclusion on Suno**

Dear Suno Team,

First, thank you. Suno is the most inspiring AI music platform I’ve experienced. The creative possibilities it unlocks are extraordinary, and I’m genuinely grateful to be part of this community.

I’m writing to share some reflections and suggestions around playlist curation and visibility. I’ve noticed that certain users and songs appear repeatedly in featured playlists, and I’ve been wondering: who curates these playlists, and what criteria are used to select songs? With so many talented creators on Suno—many of whom are paying subscribers—it can feel disheartening to see limited rotation and discoverability.

At one point, I found myself liking and commenting on songs by playlist curators, hoping to be noticed. But it didn’t feel authentic. I’d rather be included in a system that feels fair, diverse, and artistically driven. Even one feature can mean the world.

For example, I was honored when one of my songs was featured in the “Best of Suno v4.5” playlist. That moment had a huge impact—my followers doubled in two days, and the track reached over 20,000 plays. I received messages from listeners around the world. It reminded me that being heard matters.

Later, two of my songs were briefly featured—each for just 24 hours. During those short windows, the first reached 18,000 plays and the second 12,000. But once removed, the growth stalled. That drop-off shows just how crucial even small windows of visibility can be.

Afterward, I began receiving requests for likes and comments from other users, and I saw the other side of the system. I understand how overwhelming it must be for curators and influencers. I truly respect those boundaries. But it left me unsure how to be seen again—without self-promotion or pressure to perform.

At first, I engaged with other artists because I was moved by their stories. Suno’s community is full of raw, honest, deeply personal music. One creator even composed entirely through lyrics and listener feedback—despite not being able to hear the songs themselves. That touched me deeply. This platform is more than trends—it’s about connection.

That’s why I care. I want to see more unheard voices lifted up. My own brief feature inspired me to create more, to invest more, and to engage more meaningfully. But over time, I noticed my comments changed—from genuine connection to trying to be seen again. That shift made me pause.

I also noticed that after liking around 10 songs, I receive a message saying I’ve reached a limit. This shows the system can control interaction flow. But perhaps this could be refined. Instead of batching likes, maybe introduce a short pause after each one—encouraging listeners to take their time and respond thoughtfully. It would make the platform feel more musical, more mindful—and ultimately, more human.

Because music is not a scrollable feed. It isn’t instant. It requires listening, presence, time. A like-for-like culture doesn’t serve music the way it might on visual platforms. Songs carry stories. They deserve more than a quick swipe and a tap.

I don’t just want visibility—I want to reach people. My music isn’t just for dance floors (though I respect that); it’s about emotional truth, resilience, and human connection. I know it would speak to others—if they had a chance to hear it.

I hope this message is received in the spirit I intend: with respect, gratitude, and belief in Suno’s mission. I’m proud to be here. I just hope the future of visibility can be more inclusive, more curious, and more connected.

Warmly,  
**Mehmet Bagbozan**

.Subject: A Personal Reflection on Playlist Visibility and Inclusion on Suno

Dear Suno Team,

First of all, I’d like to extend my appreciation. Suno stands out as the leading AI music platform, and I truly admire the innovation and creativity it enables.

I’m writing with a few thoughts, questions, and suggestions—mainly about how playlists are curated on the platform. I’ve noticed that the same users and songs appear frequently in featured playlists. This made me wonder: who is responsible for creating these playlists, and what criteria are used in selecting songs? With so many great creators on Suno, including many paying subscribers, it feels a bit discouraging to see such limited rotation.

At one point, I found myself trying to engage with playlist curators by liking and commenting on their songs, hoping to be noticed. But over time, that felt a bit unnatural. I don’t want my presence to rely on chasing attention—it would feel far more meaningful to be included through a more diverse and inclusive system. Even one feature can mean a lot.

For example, one of my songs was once featured in the “Best of Suno v4.5” playlist. I was truly honored and grateful. The impact was incredible: my followers doubled in just two days, and the song reached over twenty thousand plays. I also received messages from around the world. That single moment gave me an enormous confidence boost—not just as a user, but as an artist.

In fact, I’ve had two of my songs featured in the “Best of Suno v4.5” playlist—but only for a very limited time. The first was visible for just twenty-four hours before being removed, and shortly after, a second song of mine was added, also for twenty-four hours. In total, my songs were featured for just forty-eight hours combined. During that short window, the first song received over eighteen thousand plays, and the second reached over twelve thousand. Since then, the combined total has only grown by about one thousand plays in the week that followed. That kind of drop-off shows just how impactful a playlist feature is—and how fleeting that exposure can be if not given time to breathe.

After being featured, I started receiving messages from others asking for support—likes, comments, listens. I suddenly saw the system from another side. I can only imagine how overwhelming that must be for playlist curators and influencers on the platform. I really do understand and respect that. But it also left me unsure of how to be considered again, without having to push or perform for attention.

In the beginning, my engagement with other creators was entirely genuine. I was moved by the stories behind their songs. There’s something deeply human about what people share through their music on Suno—it’s often raw, emotional, and deeply personal. I even came across a creator who composed songs without hearing, using only the written lyrics and listener feedback. That touched me deeply. It reminded me this platform isn’t just about trends—it’s about expression and connection.

That’s why I care—not just about being featured again myself, but about seeing all kinds of unique, unheard voices lifted up. My own feature inspired me to create more, to buy extra credits, and to engage more meaningfully with the community. But over time, I noticed that my comments and interactions started to shift—I was no longer just connecting, I was trying to be seen again. And that made me pause.

One more thing I want to make really clear. Right now, after liking around 10 songs, I get a message saying, “You’ve reached your like limit”—and I have to pause. So I know the system already has the power and technology to control how we interact. But in my opinion, that limit should apply after each song, not after 10.

Instead of letting people rush through and like 10 tracks in a row, why not slow it down just a little? For example, after liking one song, there could be a short pause—maybe 30 seconds or 1 minute—before they can like another. That would encourage people to actually listen first, think about how the song made them feel, and then decide whether to like it or not. That’s what I try to do. But when people tap 5 or 10 likes in a few seconds, I know they didn’t listen—and it creates pressure to go return the gesture, even if it wasn’t real. I believe this kind of change would gently shift the entire culture of the platform toward more thoughtful, honest engagement. And it would make the algorithm smarter and more human at the same time.

There’s one more layer to this I want to express clearly: the like-for-like culture itself doesn’t really belong on a platform like Suno. That kind of system makes sense for platforms like Instagram, Facebook, or Twitter—where you can scroll through dozens of images or posts in a minute. You can quickly read a line, glance at a picture, and know whether you want to like it. The content is visual and instant. There’s light, there’s recognition, there’s a quick response.

But music isn’t like that. You can’t decide whether you like a song just by glancing at it. You have to actually listen, often for two or three minutes, to understand how it feels and whether it resonates with you. Songs ask for emotional presence. They carry stories. They take time.

That’s why the current system—where you can like 5 or 10 songs in quick succession and then wait 30 seconds before doing it again—just doesn’t work. It encourages people to skim, like, and move on, without engaging with the music itself. If I have two hours and I genuinely want to support a hundred artists, I still don’t know if that effort will reflect in the algorithm in a way that actually helps me too. I might boost others—and I want to—but I don’t know whether anything about my visibility improves through that.

We need an algorithm that’s fair—not just fast. One that understands music is not a scrollable feed. It’s a deeper experience.

I guess what I’m trying to say is: I just want to reach more people. I also have something to say. My music isn’t just for dancing or clubbing—though I respect those, too. It’s about emotion. It’s about being honest, helping someone feel stronger, less alone, more understood. I know my music will speak to people—if only they had a chance to hear it.

I hope this message is received in the spirit it’s meant: with gratitude, honesty, and belief in the Suno vision. I appreciate the opportunity to be part of this community, and I hope for a future where visibility and recognition are more widely shared among the diverse voices that make Suno so special.

Warm regards,
Mehmet Bagbozan

### 1. **GENEL TARZ & RUH**

- **Bağlama** / **Elektro saz** – ana melodiyi ve halk ezgisi ruhunu taşır

- **Zil ve bendir** – özellikle giriş ve geçişlerde doğulu bir ambiyans verir

**Modern Enstrümanlar:**
- **Elektro gitar (wah pedallı veya hafif overdrive’lı)** – riff ve sololarda kullanılır  
- **Bas gitar** – groove'u oluşturur, Türk halk müziği ritmik yapısına göre çalınmalı  
- **Davul (Canlı / analog tınılı)** – düz rock beat ama halk ezgisi temposuyla  
- **Synth / Org (Analog tonlu)** – arka fonda hafifçe sürükleyici tonlar vermek için

- **Tempo:** Yaklaşık 85–95 BPM

- Analog kayıt hissi yarat (reverb'lü gitarlar, canlı enstrümanlar, kuru vokal)
